title: CypherWave - AuthZ & Egress Firewall Playbook Review
summary: Deep-dive on private deployment network isolation, RBAC/SSO integration, audit log retention, and KMS envelope key flow. Agreed to run a pilot with temporary canary route and provide detailed VPC/egress playbook and test plan.
topics: KMS envelope keys and HSM integration
next_steps: Redwood to provide hardened VPC diagram and egress playbook (Diego) by 2026-12-03
Customer to share sample threat model and compliance checklist (Aisha) by 2026-12-01
Schedule pilot kickoff (tentative week of 2026-12-06) - Maya to coordinate
action_items: Diego Ramos - Share hardened VPC diagram + egress playbook - 2026-12-03
Aisha Rahman - Send CypherWave compliance checklist and data residency requirements - 2026-12-01
Maya Patel - Book pilot kickoff and invite SE workshop - 2026-12-02
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We have about 50 minutes, we'll focus on the private deployment controls your security team asked for. Diego and Ruth from our side will cover infra and operations. Aisha, do you want to start with context?

[00:22] Aisha (CypherWave Sec): Yeah, thanks. Quick background — we're preparing for SOC 2 and want to validate a private VPC deployment. Key concerns: strict egress controls, SSO integration, auditability for model prompts, and KMS handling for PHI-adjacent data. Timeline is end of Q1 for pilot.

[00:45] Diego (Redwood SE): Great. I'll go through a high-level VPC layout and the ingress/egress playbook then we'll walk through authz flows. Bear with me if I mis-say a product name — our console used to be called the Console but sometimes the transcriptions show it as Redwood Control — ha.

[01:15] Liam (CTO): Just to clarify, we need the option to keep inference inside our air-gapped tier for certain agents, but allowed outbound egress to our logging/bastion.

[01:30] Priya (Cloud Infra): Our constraints: no direct internet access from model instances, NAT for controlled egress to a logging proxy, and KMS in our AZ with key policies bound to service accounts.

[01:45] Diego (Redwood SE): Understood. So the recommended pattern we use is a private subnets stack with restricted egress through an egress gateway — in customer terms that's an egress proxy cluster in your VPC. We support routing all outbound model telemetry and audit events to a customer-owned logging endpoint.

[02:10] Jonas (Network): When you say "egress gateway" is that a managed appliance or a container service we deploy?

[02:20] Diego (Redwood SE): It's container-based; we provide a reference helm chart for the proxy. You can front it with your firewall rules or route tables. For air-gapped installs we have an on-prem package that runs the same proxy.

[02:45] Aisha: Okay I want to talk specifics on firewall rules. Our network team wants a deny-by-default posture. We need to enumerate exact hosts and ports.

[03:00] Diego: Absolutely. We typically recommend three egress classes: (1) telemetry and audit -> customer logging (HTTPS, 443), (2) model artifact fetches during startup -> internal artifact repo or signed prefetch (HTTPS, 443 but limited to repo IPs), (3) optional OS/container patching -> allowlist to patch mirror or airgap update pipeline.

[03:30] Ruth (Redwood CSM): And for emergency fallback we can configure a canary route to Redwood-hosted fallback endpoints — but that only activates under a policy you define. Many customers choose to keep that off for true air-gap.

[03:50] Aisha: We really want no automatic fallback. Any stateful callback to Redwood is a non-starter.

[04:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Noted. We'll show the plan without the fallback and call out the exact flags to disable in the control plane.

[04:15] Priya: For auth, we use Okta and want SAML SSO + SCIM for provisioning. Also role-based access with least privilege — devs shouldn't access production models or logs.

[04:35] Diego: We integrate with SAML/SSO and SCIM. Our RBAC maps into your identity groups. Apologies, I might say "RBAC rules are in the Console" — the UI label sometimes is different in logs, but the mapping is straightforward: groups->roles->policies.

[04:55] Liam: Can we force MFA for any user able to roll model versions?

[05:05] Diego: Yes, that's enforced at the IdP layer. You can split duties: only a few service accounts have deploy rights, and all human accounts must be in the MFA-enforced group.

[05:25] Aisha: Audit logs — critical. We need immutable logs for all admin actions, model calls, and API keys. Retention is 7 years for certain project classes. Can Redwood push signed logs to our SIEM?

[05:45] Diego: We ship audit events to a customer endpoint using signed webhooks over TLS. For enhanced assurance we also support pushing logs to an S3-compatible endpoint with server-side encryption and object-lock for WORM. Note: sometimes the transcript spells S3 as "ess-three" in exports.

[06:10] Priya: How granular are the events? Do we get token-level usage, prompt text redaction controls, and key rotation events?

[06:25] Diego: Events include: API key creation/deletion, model version rollouts, invocation metadata (caller id, route, latency), and sampling of request/response bodies. We provide redaction hooks — you can configure to never log prompt bodies for certain projects or to hash them before export.

[06:50] Jonas: The KMS flow — does Redwood call our KMS directly, or do you store encrypted blobs? We need to ensure HSM-backed keys never leave our control.

[07:05] Diego: For private deployments we support two options: bring-your-own-KMS (we call your KMS via a customer-managed IAM role, keys never leave the KMS) or envelope encryption where Redwood manages an encrypted blob but keys are wrapped with your master key. For highly regulated customers we recommend the BYOK + HSM approach.

[07:30] Aisha: Is there an audit trail for key usage? We need Cloud KMS logs showing decrypt/unwrap operations.

[07:40] Diego: Yes, calls to KMS go through your KMS and are visible in your key audit logs. We don't have the plaintext unless you choose the other mode where Redwood holds the ephemeral key in RAM during inference — that is still memory-only and never persisted. We'll call that out in the security design doc.

[08:05] Maya: Quick check — any compliance requirements around data residency you want to highlight?

[08:15] Aisha: EU-data residency for clinical trial PII is required. Model hosts must be in eu-west-1 and backups in the same region; logs can be aggregated to our Brussels SIEM instance.

[08:30] Diego: No problem. We can pin nodes and scheduling to that region and our routing will respect data-plane locality. Note: some customers name that "region pinning" in our docs, the export may show it as "node pin".

[08:50] Liam: On failure modes, what happens when the egress proxy loses connectivity to the SIEM? Do model calls queue or fail closed?

[09:05] Diego: You can choose policy: fail-closed or buffer-and-forward. For PII-sensitive workloads we usually recommend fail-closed for audit event channels and an explicit degraded-mode flag for model inferences. We will show the config toggles in the playbook.

[09:30] Aisha: About network policies — we need L7 inspection for egress to detect data-exfil attempts. Does your proxy support outbound TLS inspection with certificate pinning to our logging endpoint?

[09:45] Diego: The proxy can do TLS passthrough or terminate for inspection; we recommend termination at the customer proxy to allow inspection, with mTLS between model nodes and the proxy. Certificate pinning is supported via your cert bundle.

[10:10] Jonas: For on-prem we want to avoid external public DNS calls. Can the artifact fetcher do internal mirror lookups only?

[10:20] Diego: Yes, the artifact fetcher can be configured to use an internal artifact repo. We also support a signed artifact bundle that you pre-stage.

[10:40] Priya: Are there any side-channels from KV cache or local disk that we should be aware of?

[10:50] Diego: KV cache is in-memory by default and should be kept ephemeral. For private installs we mount tmpfs for caches and ensure swap is disabled; we also scrub caches at shutdown. Our ops run a KVM check — apologies, I mean a cache eviction check — sometimes the words jumble in the transcript.

[11:20] Aisha: Regarding penetration testing, can we run an external pentest against the deployment? Any restrictions?

[11:30] Ruth (Redwood CSM): Yes, customers can run pentests against their dedicated/private stacks. We require a short-run plan and a safe-word. We'll provide an accommodation and a test window.

[11:45] Maya: Also we can provide an SOC 2 artifacts pack for your auditors — it's our standard set but you'll still need to map controls to your processes.

[12:00] Liam: Let's deep-dive on a sample attack: a compromised service account tries to exfiltrate prompt history. How does the playbook detect and respond?

[12:15] Diego: Detection: anomaly scoring on event volume, unusual artifact fetches, and access from unknown IPs. Response: we revoke keys, rotate the ephemeral key, move traffic to a sandboxed node pool, and alert your SecOps via SIEM. We'll include runbook steps.

[12:45] Aisha: We need SLAs on alerting and a forensic packet capture method.

[12:55] Diego: We can push PCAPs to a customer-controlled collector for the configured window. For alerting, we support webhooks, PagerDuty, and SIEM ingestion.

[13:15] Jonas: About packet capture — storing PCAPs is sensitive. We prefer short retention and controlled access.

[13:25] Maya: Noted. We'll recommend retention windows and RBAC for PCAP access.

[13:40] Ruth: Quick question on billing telemetry — many security teams want token-level billing removed from logs to avoid leakage. We have a redaction setting for billing dimensions.

[13:55] Diego: Yes, you can turn on billing redaction for designated projects. That will hash or redact user-identifiers in telemetry.

[14:10] Aisha: For key rotation frequency, we want quarterly rotation with emergency rotation within 24 hours. Can the system support that?

[14:25] Diego: Yes, and for BYOK we recommend scheduled key rotation orchestrated by your KMS; Redwood will detect new key versions and rotate envelope keys. For emergency rotation we'll support a manual trigger documented in the playbook.

[14:45] Liam: Any limitations for HSM-backed keys vs cloud KMS?

[14:55] Diego: HSM-backed keys are fine. The main difference is latency for unwrap operations — for high throughput we recommend a short-lived ephemeral key layer to avoid KMS throttling. We'll include guidance on rate-limiting and retry policies.

[15:20] Aisha: Can you outline what the security design doc will include?

[15:30] Maya: We'll deliver: VPC diagram, egress playbook with firewall ACLs, RBAC mapping doc, SSO/SCIM integration guide, KMS flow diagrams and audit log pattern, pentest rules, and runbooks for incident response.

[15:50] Priya: Great. Regarding the VPC diagram, please include exact CIDR allocations, route table examples, and sample iptables/firewall entries — our network team needs copy-paste items.

[16:10] Diego: We'll put those into the playbook. Expect explicit CIDR examples and iptables snippets.

[16:25] Jonas: For firewall rules, we want the minimum: allow outbound 443 to SIEM IPs, allow outbound to artifact repo IPs, allow NTP to internal NTP, block everything else.

[16:40] Diego: That's aligned with our recommended deny-by-default posture. We'll encode that in the template.

[16:55] Aisha: On the topic of telemetry sampling, will Redwood sample request bodies? We might need 0% sampling for certain projects.

[17:10] Diego: You can configure sampling per project. We support 0%, 1%, 100% or custom. We'll default to 0% for regulated projects.

[17:30] Liam: Does Redwood keep any copies of prompts for model improvement?

[17:40] Maya: By default, hosted training telemetry might be used to improve models but for private deployments we respect your settings — you can opt out of any training telemetry and we won't take prompt data. We'll document the exact toggles.

[17:55] Aisha: Ok good. Any known gotchas?

[18:05] Diego: One thing: ensure your Service Account IAM role has a restrictive trust policy. Sometimes in quick pilots customers over-broad the role. We'll include a recommended policy. Also watch for clock skew between nodes and KMS which can cause auth failures — NTP sanity checks are in the guide.

[18:30] Ruth: We'll also include a staging checklist for the pilot so your infra team knows the test windows and expected traffic profiles.

[18:45] Priya: On the pilot, we want to run a simulated exfil attempt and see alerting and closure. What telemetry will you provide for that test?

[18:55] Diego: We'll provide synthetic traffic generators, logs for the test, and a postmortem template. The test will validate detection, quarantine, and key rotation.

[19:15] Maya: Anything else from the security team?

[19:25] Aisha: One more — do you support signed attestations for model weights provenance? For clinical workflows we need provenance chain.

[19:40] Diego: We support signed manifests for model artifacts, and you can require signature verification at startup. We'll add that to the artifacts section.

[19:55] Liam: Timeline recap?

[20:05] Maya: Deliver playbook and VPC diagram by 12/03. Customer to share compliance checklist by 12/01. Pilot kickoff week of 12/06. Pentest window to be agreed after pilot.

[20:20] Aisha: Sounds good.

[20:30] Maya: Okay, quick recap for notes: disable automatic fallback, BYOK w/ HSM preferred, deny-by-default egress to SIEM and artifact IPs only, RBAC via Okta + SCIM, sampling set to 0% for regulated projects, retention and object-lock for audit logs, quarterly key rotation plus emergency rotation, pilot plan to validate exfil detection.

[20:55] Liam: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the checklist and an internal sign-off.

[21:05] Maya: Thanks all — we'll send the docs and schedule the kickoff.

[21:15] (call ends)

Note: transcript includes occasional mis-hearings and shorthand common in automated transcriptions, e.g., "node pin" vs "region pinning", "ess-three" for S3, and swapped words.
